claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Changing the cooling rate after thermo-mechanical processing alters precipitate size and spatial distribution.
Rapid cooling after processing produces a fine, homogeneous precipitate distribution.
Slower cooling produces greater precipitate coarsening than rapid cooling.
Nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Nanoscale precipitates impede crack initiation.
Rapid cooling preserves small, uniformly distributed precipitates.
Small, uniformly distributed precipitates enhance plasticity.
Small, uniformly distributed precipitates delay crack propagation and thereby promote toughness.
Precipitate coarsening reduces the ability of precipitates to blunt crack tips.
Reduced crack-tip blunting caused by precipitate coarsening results in toughness loss.
Rapidly cooled specimens will retain higher toughness than the stated baseline.
Slower cooling will produce larger, coarser precipitates.
Slower cooling will reduce fracture toughness values.
Slower cooling will cause earlier crack initiation under comparable stress.
The current standard processing route uses rapid cooling and yields both a fine precipitate distribution and high toughness.
The proposed behavior applies to HEAs with similar chemical complexity and processing histories within the studied temperature and cooling-rate regime.
The proposed behavior may fail when phase transformations or other defect mechanisms dominate toughness.
The quantitative effect of cooling rate on precipitate coarsening and toughness depends on alloy composition and processing details.
Grain-boundary characteristics may also contribute to toughness variations.

contradictions.description: Rapid cooling is predicted to give higher toughness than the baseline, but the baseline is itself defined as the current rapid-cooling route that already yields a fine precipitate distribution and high toughness. No distinct rapid-cooling treatment or rate is specified, making the comparison internally inconsistent.
